title: Baal and the Sea
paragraphs: The Ugaritic Baal Cycle opens in disorder. Yam, the sea, also called Judge River, sends envoys to El's assembly to demand kingship and Baal's surrender. The gods lower their heads, and El seems ready to grant the claim. Baal alone refuses to submit. The tablet is broken at this point, so the first moves of the quarrel must be inferred from later speeches. The poem begins with a political crisis, not a creation.

Baal goes to Kothar-wa-Khasis, the craftsman god, who makes two weapons for him: Yagrush, 'Chaser', and Ayyamur, 'Driver'. The names suggest driving and pursuit. Kothar promises that Baal will strike down Yam and win everlasting kingship. The passage is damaged, and the order of the speeches has been reconstructed by scholars. His workshop is not described in detail.

The battle is told in short, formulaic lines. Baal strikes Yam with one club, then with the other. The sea is beaten down, and Baal is proclaimed king. The tablet breaks off around the victory, and the sequence of blows has to be restored from parallel lines and the logic of the poem. The victory is real, but the text does not let us watch it whole.

The story makes Baal the champion of order against a chaotic sea, but it also shows that kingship must be granted and defended. El's authority remains real even when Baal wins. Later biblical poetry uses similar imagery when Yahweh defeats the sea, which shows how widely this combat motif traveled across the ancient Near East. The myth is about power, not only weather.
notes: The opening of the Baal Cycle is damaged; the order of the first battle and the exact terms of Yam's demand are reconstructed.

title: The House of Cedar
paragraphs: After defeating Yam, Baal holds a feast on Mount Sapan. The other gods have houses, but Baal has none, and he is ashamed before his guests. He asks Anat, his sister and ally, to plead with El for a palace. Anat agrees, and the poem turns from battle to diplomacy. The house is not a private home but a sign that his rule is acknowledged.

Anat goes to El and uses a mixture of threats and flattery. The old patriarch resists at first, but she seizes him and demands a house for Baal. El yields. Anat then visits Athirat, also called Asherah, and asks the mother goddess to add her voice. The transitions between these scenes are damaged.

Kothar-wa-Khasis is summoned. He cuts cedars in Lebanon and Anti-Lebanon and builds a palace whose walls, doors, and fittings the poem describes in broken, formulaic lines. Modern retellings often add details that the tablets do not preserve, such as the number of rooms or the exact materials. Cedar was a luxury wood associated with temples and palaces.

At first Baal rejects the idea of a window; later he calls for one and opens it himself, and thunder answers. The window episode is much discussed: it may be an architectural feature, a cultic opening, or a narrative device for Baal's voice. The dedication scene is partly broken, so his enthronement is not fully preserved.
notes: The palace and window episode is fragmentary; Asherah's role and the architectural details are debated.

title: Baal and Mot
paragraphs: Mot, Death, holds sway in the underworld and is called the beloved of El. Word comes that Baal must go down to him, and Baal is afraid. Before he descends, he mates with a heifer, and a bull-calf is born; the episode is usually read as a last act of fertility before the world loses its rain. The poem gives no explanation for Mot's claim, only its inevitability.

Baal goes down into Mot's throat, and the text describes the earth turning dry. El mourns: he pours dust on his head, cuts his skin, and cries for Baal. El's grief is the grief of a father and a king. The rains stop, the fields fail, and the other gods grieve. This is the drought at the heart of the cycle.

Anat searches for Baal. When she learns what Mot has done, she confronts him, seizes him, and kills him with a sword. She winnows his body, burns it, grinds it, and sows the remains in the field. Her rage is both loyal and terrifying. The violence is shocking, and the text is damaged enough that some details remain uncertain.

Baal returns, though the text does not make the manner clear. El dreams of rain and abundance; the heavens rain oil and the wadis flow with honey. Mot also reappears, and Shapshu, the sun goddess, intervenes. The ending is partly reconstructed: the final lines are broken, and later retellings differ. The victory over death is not final.
notes: The ending of the Baal–Mot cycle is damaged; Baal's return and Anat's actions are partly reconstructed.

title: El's Feast and the Gracious Gods
paragraphs: The text known as The Gracious Gods (KTU 1.23) is not a connected epic but a ritual poem with repeated refrains and possible stage directions. It begins with El at a banquet, or perhaps in the wilderness, and the poetry is difficult enough that translators disagree about who is present and what is being celebrated. The tablet is often read as a ritual for the birth of the gods.

Two women appear, and El lies with them. They bear Shahar and Shalim, whose names are usually translated Dawn and Dusk. The identity of the women is unclear; some scholars read one as Athirat, but the damaged tablet does not settle the question. The birth is both a cosmic event and a ritual one.

The poem then turns to the gracious gods themselves and to the offerings that accompany their story. It gives them a place in the landscape and in the ritual, but the transitions are abrupt and repeated lines may belong to different performers. Some lines may be instructions for a rite rather than narrative.

The text ends with directions for recitation and sacrifice, which suggests that it was performed. Shahar and Shalim appear rarely elsewhere, but here they are the children of El and the focus of a rite. The fragmentary state means that any retelling is a cautious reconstruction, not a fixed story. Its poetry resists a smooth narrative.
notes: KTU 1.23 is difficult and damaged; the speakers, ritual setting and the births of the gracious gods are debated.

title: Kirta and the Heir
paragraphs: Kirta, a king whose household has been destroyed, has lost his wife and children. The opening is broken, but his grief is clear: his house is empty, and he has no heir. He weeps in his chamber until El, the father of the gods, takes pity on him and appears in a dream. The text gives no reason for the disaster.

El tells Kirta to wash, sacrifice, and march on Udum, the city of King Pabil. He must demand Pabil's daughter Hurray as his wife. Kirta follows the instructions, and Pabil, after some negotiation, agrees. Hurray comes to Kirta, and El blesses the union with sons. The poem lingers on the wedding and the birth of the heir.

The blessing does not end the story. Kirta falls ill, and the text hints that a vow to Asherah was left unpaid. His household mourns him, and his youngest son Yassib raises the question of succession. Kirta answers with a curse, and the poem explores what happens when a king can no longer rule. Illness here is also a political crisis.

El sends a healer who drives the illness from Kirta's body, and the king seems to recover. The tablets then break off before the succession is settled, and the ending is lost rather than merely obscure. Later retellings often supply a harmonious close; the surviving text does not. Whether Kirta names an heir remains unknown.
notes: The Kirta epic breaks off; the ending and the question of succession are lost or disputed.

title: Aqhat and the Bow
paragraphs: Danel, a righteous judge and a man of the Rephaim, has no son. He gives food and drink to the gods for seven days, and Baal intercedes for him. El blesses Danel, and his wife conceives. The birth of Aqhat is the answer to a long childlessness. The story opens with patience and ritual.

When Aqhat grows up, Danel gives him a bow and arrows. Anat sees the bow at a feast and wants it. She offers Aqhat silver, gold, and perhaps even immortality, but he refuses, saying that a bow belongs to a man, not to a goddess. The refusal is blunt, and it costs him his life. His refusal is also a claim about gender and status.

Anat does not forget. She goes to El, and the killing follows; the relevant lines are broken. She sends the warrior Yatpan, who strikes Aqhat down. Aqhat dies, and drought follows: the dew fails, the rain stops, and the fields dry. Danel mourns for his son. The land suffers with the family. The drought is both natural and moral.

In the surviving sequel, Aqhat's sister Pughat sets out to avenge him, but the tablets break off before the story is complete. The ending is lost or disputed, and interpreters disagree about whether Pughat succeeds and how the drought is lifted. The bow's meaning is also debated. No complete copy of the epic survives.
notes: The Aqhat epic is incomplete; the ending and the reason for the drought are disputed.
